Yes. 

The central turn in the story—watching Q’s effortless charm completely fail him as he attempts to fire his subordinate, Meredith—is both surprising and appropriate. 

It is **surprising** because the first half of the story carefully establishes Q as a "golden boy" with a "preternatural inability to experience social friction." The narrator sets up the expectation that Q can charm his way out of any negligence (like his forgotten 20-page paper) and make people feel grateful even when he is hurting them (like his ex-girlfriend Clara). Seeing him sweat, crack his voice, and look "entirely pathetic" subverts the mythical image the narrator has held onto for a decade.

At the same time, the turn is **appropriate** because Q is behaving in the exact same way he always has—relying on smooth talk, vague flattery, and conflict avoidance rather than doing the actual work. It makes complete sense within the reality of the story that techniques which worked on infatuated college girlfriends and pretentious lecturers in his twenties would fail miserably in the real world of corporate finance when deployed against a sharp, prepared professional whose livelihood is at stake. His downfall isn't caused by an out-of-character mistake, but rather by his core character traits finally meeting an environment where they no longer work.
